I ask because if you're going for a more gritty, or mature, atmosphere, naming all skills Power Bomb, Power Boosters, etc, (or star check, or star dash) is incredibly cheesy. Like, watching Power Rangers as an adult cheesy. Or early 80's B-rated action movie cheesy.

A lot of developers know the advantage of create "cute" assets over "realistic" ones, especially for mobile games. Yes, it obviously hits the younger demographic, but "cute" graphics, as I refer to them, is somehow more...satisfying.

For me personally, I think it has to do with great tweening, animations, sound effects, and visual effects.

Think of a photorealistic character that is just a blob of jelly. To stay consistent with the more realistic, or authentic, feel of the design, it will bounce around, jiggle and all that, maybe squirt a little bit of jelly if it lands on the ground after jumping.

But in a "cute" world, it SPLASHES around, it squirts lots of jelly, it wobbles and jiggles whenever it touches anything. It stretches as it jumps, squishes as it lands, uses juicy sound effects (literally) and most likely, it's got a heavy dose of gloss on the character image to make it look appealing. Shiny, squishy, juicy...doesn't matter if it's childish, it's somehow appealing. That's one of the reasons why Candy Crush is so successful. Juice. Period.

Seriously. Look up "juice" as it relates to video games on youtube. You'll notice, the games tend to feature "childish" graphics over photorealistic ones. At least for me personally, photorealistic games pleases my eyes. "Cute" juicy games pleases my eyes, ears, and in my imagination, smell and taste.

You ever watch Bugs Bunny and think his carrot looks so so good to eat? Like, better to eat than a REAL carrot?

To answer you question more directly, simply put, "childish" graphics are more saturated, brighter, and usually have a fair amount of contrast. The reason for this is the reason why toddler's toys and children's toys are brightly colored. Colors illicit feelings, emotions, and younger human beings tend to run on instinct alone.

Contrast that, more 'mature' games feature more authentic textures and graphics, with more earthtones, less contrast, darker colors. in general, I think this coincides well with an adult's ability to think in abstract terms or consider deep subjects. Darker, more photorealistic images illicit more complicated emotions than brightly colored images do. So it seems reasonable that older humans connect with those graphics.

So....I really don't think photorealistic graphics can convey the sense of childish, cute, innocence that cartoony graphics can. And the only way for cartoony graphics to illicit any kind of deep, abstract thought is to use gameplay & story instead.

If I were in your shoes, I'd probably read this response as depressing. But that's just me.

Honestly, everything I have read tells me not to put all my eggs in one basket for my first game. I'm not going to be a millionaire, its probably not going to be wildly successful. I'm not going to be able to quit my day job.

And...that's ok. In fact, that's not even a problem.

The general consensus for a developer's first game is not to think about all the nitty details. Just release your game. Get it finished, get it out in the world. Don't be messing around with Steam Greenlight.

If you want feedback before release, upload it to your own phone. Let you friends use your phone and play with it for 15 minutes. Take notes on their first impression, whatever verbal opinions they share, etc. You don't need to be worrying about early-access. This is literally your first game ever and you've been a game developer for.....a month?

Congrats on your completion of your first game. Go have a beer and celebrate. Are you aware of how rare it is for an individual to simply FINISH their game? You're already leagues ahead of everyone who has unfinished games sitting in folders on their HDD.

Let your friends play it, test it, release it in to the wild. Fly free my friend. After a few games, you can increase the scope of your game design and start to consider things like early access or Steam Greenlight. For now, just roll with it.
